candidate.answerReason: The figure places announcements 1 through 10 consecutively around the circle. Translating the odd announcements into neighboring sums and following the even positions gives 2x_6+8=10, so the requested pick is uniquely 1.

methods.label: Follow one unknown around the circle
methods.explanation:
Each announcement gives the sum of the two neighboring picks: the sum is twice the announced average. Starting with the desired pick, we can therefore express successive picks in terms of just one unknown.

[Figure 1](figures/1990_AMC_12_Q26_question_fig1.svg)

The announcements appear in the order \(1,2,\ldots,10\) around the circle. Let \(x_i\) denote the original number picked by the person announcing \(i\), and set \(x_6=t\). The person announcing \(7\) has neighbors who picked \(x_6\) and \(x_8\), so \(x_6+x_8=14\). Continuing through announcements \(9,1,3\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_8&=14-t,\\
x_{10}&=18-x_8=4+t,\\
x_2&=2-x_{10}=-2-t,\\
x_4&=6-x_2=8+t.
\end{aligned}
\]
This follows every other position until we reach the other neighbor of the person announcing \(5\). That announcement requires \(x_4+x_6=10\), hence
\[
8+t+t=10,
\qquad 2t=2,
\qquad t=1.
\]
Every set of picks satisfying the announcements must give this value of \(t\). Thus the requested number is uniquely \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
methods.levelReason: Successively expressing quantities in one unknown and solving the resulting linear equation uses elementary school algebra, within the AMC 12 scope.

methods.label: Combine sums to cancel unwanted picks
methods.explanation:
Twice an announced average is the sum of the neighboring picks. Rather than finding each pick, we can add and subtract these sums to leave only the desired one.

[Figure 1](figures/1990_AMC_12_Q26_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(x_i\) be the original pick of the person announcing \(i\). Since the announcements run consecutively around the circle, the odd announcements give
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{10}+x_2&=2,\\
x_2+x_4&=6,\\
x_4+x_6&=10,\\
x_6+x_8&=14,\\
x_8+x_{10}&=18.
\end{aligned}
\]
The equations from announcements \(5\) and \(7\) together contain \(2x_6+x_4+x_8\). Subtracting the equations from announcements \(3\) and \(9\) removes \(x_4\) and \(x_8\), but leaves \(-x_2-x_{10}\). Adding the equation from announcement \(1\) removes those remaining unwanted terms. Therefore
\[
2x_6=10+14-6-18+2=2.
\]
Dividing by \(2\) gives \(x_6=1\). This identity holds for every set of picks consistent with the announcements, so the requested number is uniquely \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses the arithmetic-mean definition and addition-subtraction elimination with matching coefficients. It requires no general theory of linear systems.

candidate.annotationRationale: Interpreting arithmetic means as neighboring sums is the specific catalog target common to both routes. Writing expressions, combining like terms, preserving equality, and signed addition-subtraction support both methods. The one-variable modeling procedure cnm_045 belongs only to the first method, which expresses all relevant picks using t and solves one linear equation with cnm_042. The second method instead introduces several unknown picks and combines their equations, using cnm_090 and cnm_036. These alternative procedures are method-local and are not joint requirements. The annotations do not establish student mastery.

Method 2 correctly cancels all other picks to give 2x6=10+14-6-18+2=2. Both establish the requested value uniquely, and the announcements are consistent.
